title: Do Not Mitigate
summary: Do Not Mitigate is less a control than a documented decision not to apply one, recorded where a fix would cost more than the behaviour it targets. It appears in threat modelling and risk registers when a defensive change would break an availability-critical process, destabilise an undocumented legacy system, or push attackers into a quieter path that current monitoring cannot see. The practical alternative is compensating work: stronger detection, tighter monitoring, segmentation, rehearsal and a named risk owner who accepts the exposure for a stated period. Evidence includes the risk entry itself, the technical rationale, the approver, the review date and the detection rule that was written instead of the fix. This is a governance artefact, and auditors read it as a sign of deliberate risk management rather than neglect.

beginner.definition: Sometimes the safest choice is to leave a system as it is on purpose. Do Not Mitigate describes those situations, where a change could break something important or create a new danger. Instead of blocking the behaviour, you watch for it closely and plan how to respond. The decision is written down, with a reason and an owner.
beginner.whyItMatters: Not every weakness has a safe fix, and pretending otherwise can cause an outage. A rushed change to a hospital system or a factory controller can hurt people, not just data. It can also destroy the clues you need during an investigation. Recording a deliberate decision keeps that risk visible instead of forgotten. It also forces you to put detection in place, so the risk is managed rather than ignored.
howItWorks: Describe the technique and the affected system in plain terms, including what it does for the business.
List the realistic fixes and explain what each one would break, slow down or cost.
Write down the compensating controls you will use, such as monitoring, alerts and isolation.
Name a person who accepts the remaining risk and set a date to look at it again.
Prepare a rehearsed response, so the team knows what to do when the behaviour appears.
Review the decision on schedule and close it as soon as a safe fix becomes available.
beginner.example: A small clinic keeps an old record system running overnight because it holds years of patient notes. Shutting it down every time something odd appears would be unsafe. Instead the staff log every unusual event, keep the machine on its own network, and review the decision each quarter. The risk is known, watched and owned, not forgotten.
takeaways: Deciding not to fix something is acceptable when it is written down, justified and reviewed.
Every accepted risk needs compensating detection and a named owner with a review date.
Never let an accepted risk quietly become an unmanaged one as staff and systems change.

objectives: Explain when declining to apply a mitigation is a defensible security decision.
Describe the elements of a complete documented risk acceptance.
Match compensating controls such as monitoring and segmentation to an accepted risk.
Recognise the operational harms that make an aggressive fix counterproductive.
Outline a review cycle that retires accepted risks when safe fixes appear.
